text: NN/g recommends using AI to draft study questions and documentation, with expert review: generated usability tasks can lead or prime participants even when the prompt includes examples and guidance. (low confidence)

text: The QualAnalyzer paper demonstrates process traceability by preserving segment-level inputs, instructions and outputs; in its interview-coding case study, classifications and quoted supporting passages make individual coding decisions inspectable. This is a methodological example, not evidence that the software remains publicly installable. (low confidence)

text: Use AI-generated codes and clusters as a preliminary analysis that researchers inspect and revise. NN/g reports missed transcript sections and inappropriate tags; the QualAnalyzer paper likewise assigns interpretation and the defensibility of findings to the researcher. (medium confidence)

text: MeasuringU’s review reports mixed empirical alignment: some synthetic results match means, correlations or factor structures, while others show reduced variation, distorted relationships or shallow narratives. Its conclusion is narrower than universal failure: occasional agreement does not yet justify relying on synthetic research for critical decisions. (low confidence)

text: NN/g recommends AI for drafting research goals, interview or survey questions, test plans, and study documentation, while warning about invented sources and violations of research best practices. (low confidence)

text: AI assistance with study planning and analysis should be distinguished from replacing participants: the former works on research tasks and collected data, while synthetic interviews generate simulated accounts rather than observed human experiences. NN/g recommends supplementing real-user research rather than substituting synthetic users. (medium confidence)

text: Treat synthetic output as explicitly labeled hypotheses for later human research, rather than presenting it as participant evidence. NN/g recommends hypothesis maps and clear provenance; Synthetic User Council describes its own role as challenging a research brief before real interviews. (medium confidence)
keywords: AI-assisted UX research and synthetic participant validity

text: An audit trail or repeatable model output does not establish correctness. QualAnalyzer warns that consistent coding can systematically diverge from human judgment; MeasuringU similarly reports that correlated synthetic and human responses can still differ systematically. (medium confidence)
keywords: AI-assisted UX research and synthetic participant validity

text: In Simulacrum of Stories, Kapania and colleagues interviewed 19 qualitative researchers and asked them to recreate familiar interviews with an LLM probe. Initial narrative resemblance gave way to concerns about contextual depth, ambiguous epistemic position, researcher positionality, participant consent and agency, community erasure, and qualitative research legitimacy. This is evidence about researcher experience and epistemology, not a population-wide accuracy benchmark. (low confidence)
keywords: AI-assisted UX research and synthetic participant validity

text: Synthetic participants can reproduce dominant perspectives while obscuring the people they purport to represent. Kapania and colleagues describe displacement and distortion of community voices; Russell cautions that biased or insufficiently diverse training data can skew simulated insights away from the intended user population. (medium confidence)
keywords: AI-assisted UX research and synthetic participant validity

text: Synthetic User Council’s repository whitepaper positions the system as a preparation tool that proposes blind spots, challenged assumptions, interview questions and recruitment priorities. That stated purpose is not independent validation that its simulated personas predict real participants. (low confidence)
keywords: AI-assisted UX research and synthetic participant validity

text: Validity claims must stay tied to the task, population, model, prompt and settings tested. MeasuringU warns that these vary across studies and change over time; Russell calls for validation against real-world human data. A successful replication should not be generalized to untested populations or UX decisions. (medium confidence)
keywords: AI-assisted UX research and synthetic participant validity

text: Human review must actively examine the data and interpretations. QualAnalyzer warns that preserving prompts and outputs can create an unused audit trail; NN/g recommends checking primary sources and reviewing suggested qualitative codes for misunderstanding. (medium confidence)
keywords: AI-assisted UX research and synthetic participant validity

text: The Simulacrum of Stories study identifies confirmation-bias and representation risks: researcher-selected persona traits shape responses, and repeated prompting can tune simulated data toward researcher expectations. (low confidence)
keywords: AI-assisted UX research and synthetic participant validity

text: MeasuringU’s review reports mixed results: some synthetic responses correlate with human responses, but reduced variance, incorrect averages or statistical relationships, and shallow narratives can coexist with that apparent agreement. Correlation alone does not establish interchangeability. (low confidence)
keywords: AI-assisted UX research and synthetic participant validity

text: QualAnalyzer’s authors distinguish auditability and repeatability from validity: consistent model outputs may still diverge systematically from human judgments, and an audit trail requires active human scrutiny. (low confidence)

text: Protocol rehearsal and challenging a research brief are bounded proposed uses for synthetic participants; the Simulacrum study also warns that rehearsal can steer researchers toward model-suggested directions, so these uses do not establish participant replacement validity. (medium confidence)
